To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of a heat pump with an air-to-air heat recovery device to provide heat for a food drying process is not currently economically feasible.

the use of heat pump air-to-air heat recovery is attractive for food industry dry operations if the HP is designed for the lowest possible evaporator temperature and the heat recovery is combined with a heat exchanger.

the transcritical heat pump is a thermodynamically well matched heat recovery option for food spray dryers but that the capital cost is high and the energy efficiency low, so that it is only attractive for very low inlet air temperatures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of heat pump heat recovery in food drying.
the design and operation of a heat pump heat recovery system that can provide significant energy savings for a typical spray drying application in the dairy industry.
a new concept of heat pump heat recovery for drying processes, which is based on the combination of an AHX and an HP.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HP heat recovery is attractive for spray dryers with inlet air temperature above about 200 °C, and with evaporation temperatures of 20–30 °C or lower.
heat pump heat recovery is not economically attractive for a typical spray drying process in New Zealand, although it may be attractive for other processes.
heat pump heat recovery is attractive for the food industry dryer only in special situations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the heat pump heat recovery system has a potential to provide significant energy cost savings for a spray dryer, but the capital cost of a heat pump system needs to be reduced by a factor of 3 or more to make it attractive for the New Zealand food industry.
heat recovery is an attractive option for spray dryers in New Zealand, and heat pumps could be used for further heat recovery, but only if HP costs could be reduced.

for a typical New Zealand spray dryer, the best option for heat recovery is to use an AHX to heat inlet ambient air to 200 ° C and then to use the exhaust air at 76 °C, 38.5% RH to provide up to 30% of the air inlet heating load with a heat pump with R134a as the refrigerant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
heat pump heat recovery is a promising option to reduce energy consumption in food drying.
the heat pump cycle can be designed to match the heat recovery needs of a typical food spray dryer, with a COP of up to 4.5 and a heat recovery of up to 40% possible.
heat pumps can provide a good energy saving opportunity for the food industry.
